sources.headline: Netanyahu’s new security doctrine: Regional strategy or election ploy?
sources.text: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has unveiled an updated national security doctrine and displayed a map of rival regional alignments, signalling a security approach that prioritises preemptive military action, the expansion of buffer zones, and the pursuit of new regional partnerships.The document was developed with the assistance of Israel’s National Security Council and published by the Prime Minister’s Office on Sunday, just nine days before Israel’s parliamentary elections that could spell the end of Netanyahu’s time in office. It outlines a formal policy of preventing perceived threats through military action rather than containment – a policy that has already been seen in action over the past few years, as Israel pursues multiple wars and attacks on its neighbours.Electoral survival strategyThe timing of the map’s release carries particular political significance, with Netanyahu fighting to retain power amid criticism of his conduct in power, the ongoing corruption trial he faces and his handling of the October 7, 2023, attacks, as well as the wars that followed.Recommended Stories list of 3 itemslist 1 of 3Famine fears as aid cuts and shipment restrictions coincide in Gazalist 2 of 3Russia’s Lavrov discusses US war and regional security during Tehran visitlist 3 of 3Houthi attack on Yemen army camp in Shabwa kills at least 53: reportsend of listAs the October 27 election day draws closer, Netanyahu is attempting to bolster his credentials as Israel’s ‘Mr Security’, hoping to get the votes of Israelis who may not like some of his other policies or behaviour, but still view him as the most likely leader to defend the country.Netanyahu, who did get the endorsement of US President Donald Trump on Sunday, said during the briefing that Israel could face the possibility of a far less supportive administration in Washington in two years, after the end of the Trump presidency.“In two years, a president… who is extremely hostile to Israel could come to power [in the United States],” Netanyahu warned.He therefore argued that Israel must “expand our network of alliances and develop capabilities that make us a valuable asset” to other countries as a way of protecting itself if US policy towards it changed.The comments, according to analysts, suggest that Netanyahu is seeking to portray his leadership as essential to navigating both Israel’s regional military challenges and its diplomatic isolation, all while keeping a fearful electorate reassured.Mohanad Hage Ali, deputy director for research at the Malcolm H Kerr Carnegie Middle East Center, explained that the strategic presentation centred on competing regional blocs and buffer zones.That framework “incubates and nurtures existential fears, which would lead Israeli voters to feel the need for a decisive leader”, Hage Ali noted.In his assessment, Netanyahu stands to benefit from the Israeli public’s fear of regional threats by presenting himself as a familiar leader capable of managing them, making him “the devil you know”, as the analyst put it, to voters reluctant to embrace political change at a sensitive time.Netanyahu’s political opponents have been quick to push back against that narrative.Gadi Eisenkot, one of the prime minister’s main challengers in the upcoming election, said that the published doctrine was “two hollow pages, full of slogans that have nothing to do with a security concept”.Another, former Prime Minister Yair Lapid, described the document as “superficial”.Expanding security zonesThe map displayed during Netanyahu’s briefing was originally published in May by Friedrich-Ebert-Stiftung, a German political foundation. It divides the Middle East and parts of Africa into competing blocs, highlighting the region’s complex network of alliances and rivalries.Those networks include states, unrecognised entities and non-state actors.The map identifies an Israel-United Arab Emirates alignment, described as the “Hexagon Alliance”, alongside a separate grouping of Egypt, Turkiye, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia – the latter three of which signed the Mecca mutual defence pact in August – labelled the “Sunni Diamond Alliance”. It also depicts Iran and its regional allies as a separate axis.The map serves to illustrate the issues outlined in the published security doctrine, presenting a region where Israel faces multiple threats, the alliance that Israel is seeking to cultivate across the wider region, and the perceived need for “buffer zones” – the occupation of territory in other countries.Israel’s existing illegal occupation of territory in Gaza and southern Lebanon illustrates the potential consequences of expanding the buffer zone approach.Hage Ali warned that continuing to pursue an approach built around expanding military control could lead to “more conflict and more ethnic cleansing” under the guise of security buffers.Embracing regional factionsA striking element of the map displayed by Netanyahu is its explicit designation of non-state actors as friendly entities.The map highlights territories controlled by the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces in Sudan and Khalifa Haftar’s self-styled Libyan National Army within an alignment deemed cooperative to Israel and the United Arab Emirates.Israel views these actors as pragmatic partners or at least cooperative entities in a broader strategic grid, Hage Ali explained. However, the public association of these groups with Israel threatens to damage their domestic standing across the Arab world.That reflects Netanyahu’s immediate priorities, where “what Israelis think matters more than the reputation of your allies and the viability of these alliances”, Hage Ali added.The portrayal of the Middle East as a region divided into competing alliances also carries risks for Netanyahu’s broader diplomatic ambitions.Earlier this year, Netanyahu proposed a “hexagon of alliances”, envisaging cooperation between Israel, India, Greece, Cyprus and unnamed Arab, African and Asian partners, against what he described as “radical” regional alliances.The proposed grouping has not been established as a formal alliance, and commentators in Israel and the international press have described the project as a branding exercise rather than a binding military pact, noting that countries like India prioritise non-alignment and pragmatic trade over ideologically rigid blocs.For Tehran and its regional partners, the map also offers potent political leverage.Hage Ali emphasised that the visual layout “will certainly help their propaganda machine”, providing Hezbollah and other Iranian allies with evidence to reinforce the narrative that Israel seeks to expand and dominate the region.

sources.headline: Trump endorses embattled Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for reelection
sources.text:
FILE - President Donald Trump listens as Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu speaks at President Donald Trump's Mar-a-Lago club, Dec. 29, 2025, in Palm Beach, Fla.
Alex Brandon/AP
hide caption
Alex Brandon/AP
WEST PALM BEACH, Fla. — President Donald Trump on Sunday endorsed embattled Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu late in his reelection campaign, a coveted boost because of Trump's popularity but one that the American had withheld for months as the vote neared and the leaders' strategies in the Middle East diverged.
Trump said in a post on social media that Netanyahu "has been a Great Warrior Prime Minister, and an even greater Partner for Peace in combatting the Islamic Republic of Iran." Israelis are set to vote Oct. 27, in the first national elections since Hamas attacked Israel on Oct. 7, 2023. The absence of an endorsement was a setback for the Likud politician, who had billed his tight ties to the Republican president as a selling point for staying in power. "Thank you, President Trump, for the tremendous support and work together," Netanyahu said in a statement in Hebrew posted on X. "Together we will complete the mission!"
His Likud Party attached to the statement a 35-second video showing clips of the two leaders together and Trump praising Netanyahu. It was not immediately clear what impact the endorsement would have on what is expected to be a tight race. Trump is still popular in Israel, but many Israelis, including leading commentators, have expressed disappointment over the inconclusive outcome of the Iran war and Trump's ceasefire proposal, which fell short of many of the countries' key goals when they jointly launched the war in February.
In his post, Trump again threatened to "soon finish the job" against Iran "unless they change their ways, rapidly," but added he might not want to if Netanyahu loses the election. "If Israel has the wrong Leader, which would be anyone other than Bibi, America will have to do this work ourselves, and I am not inclined to do so," Trump said. He said Netanyahu had been "Strong, Brave, and Brilliant in the face of tremendous opposition, including that coming from even Israel, itself." Trump endorsed Netanyahu in past elections and in November he sent a letter to Israeli President Isaac Herzog asking him to pardon Netanyahu on corruption charges. But Trump's comments about Netanyahu in recent months had been much more subdued, and he repeatedly demurred when asking if he would back the prime minister. The president, when asked in a Time magazine interview published this month about backing the Israeli leader, said, "I'm not involved in politics anymore," despite his campaigning for and endorsing U.S. politicians.
Trump, especially in his second term, has sought to give his stamp of approval to candidates in foreign elections and claimed credit when they have been successful. He endorsed Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán in his unsuccessful bid for a fifth term, as well as Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi and Polish President Karol Nawrocki, and several Latin American leaders. Trump and Netanyahu have been close allies and seemed more aligned than ever in the wake of the joint U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran's nuclear facilities in 2025. But over the course of the nearly eight-month war with Iran this year, they have had disagreements.
Trump criticized Israel's decision to attack a key Iranian gas field in the first weeks of the war. In June, he called Netanyahu "crazy." Trump also said that he was "a little bit perturbed" as Israel's fighting with Hezbollah militants in Lebanon was holding back peace talks with Iran. Beyond Iran, Netanyahu in August rejected Trump's latest plan to advance a stalled ceasefire in Gaza, pushing back on the U.S. administration's call for Israel to withdraw from territory it controls in Gaza until Hamas has been disarmed.

Trump endorses embattled Israeli PM Netanyahu ahead of October 27 election 
 
  Middle East   
 US President Donald Trump on Sunday endorsed Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ahead of Israel's October 27 elections. It was not clear what impact the endorsement would have on voters, since many Israelis have expressed disappointment with Trump over the outcome of the Iran war and the US president's ceasefire proposal.   
 
 
 
 
Issued on: 18/10/2026 - 18:25Modified: 19/10/2026 - 07:24
    4 min Reading time   
  Share     
 
  By:  
 
  FRANCE 24       
 
     
 A file image of US President Donald Trump with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in Palm Beach, Florida, on December 29, 2025. © Jonathan Ernst, Reuters    
 
US President Donald Trump endorsed on Sunday his ally Benjamin Netanyahu before Israel's close-fought parliamentary election on October 27, providing a boost to the veteran prime minister's bid to win a new mandate. 
Netanyahu touted his close relationship with the US president in a video released by his Likud party, saying that together they had "crushed Iran" and adding that re-election would allow him to work with Trump to "elminate the Iranian threat over the next two years, or even sooner". 
The endorsement comes less than two weeks before Israel's first vote since the October 7, 2023 Hamas-led attack, which opposition politicians have accused Netanyahu of bearing personal responsibility for after allegedly ignoring warnings. 
Polls show Netanyahu is in a tight election race. He has worked closely with Trump on Israel's multi-front wars after the Hamas-led attack, including when bombarding Iran, and the endorsement could be a boon to his re-election campaign. 
"Bibi Netanyahu has been Strong, Brave, and Brilliant in the face of tremendous opposition, including that coming from even Israel, itself," Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform, using a common nickname for the Israeli leader. 
"This is the kind of Partner that the United States of America is demanding of Israel, a Country for which it has done so much. Please let this Letter serve to represent my Complete and Total Endorsement of Bibi Netanyahu in his upcoming Race for Re-Election as Prime Minister of Israel." 
Read moreHow Netanyahu survived the political fallout from the October 7 attacks 
The election is seen as a referendum on Netanyahu, who quickly thanked the US leader for his support on Sunday. 
"Thank you, President Trump, for your tremendous support and for our work together. Together we will complete the mission!" he wrote on X. 
"I ask you to listen carefully to what President Trump said this evening," Netanyahu told voters. "He said that together we have accomplished extraordinary things... But there is still a mission to complete." 
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi warned Netanyahu was "driving America into another war". 
"Last time you wanted to 'finish the job', Iran emerged even stronger. Want to try your luck again? Be our guest. But be careful; we have unfinished jobs too," Araghchi wrote on X. 
Trump joined Netanyahu in a US-Israeli attack on Iran in late February but agreed to a ceasefire in April in the face of widespread US public opposition to the war, which had sent oil prices spiralling. 
Speaking at an event in August, Netanyahu said Trump "is our greatest friend, one of the greatest friends we have had in the White House". 
But relations between the two have at times been strained on Iran, with Netanyahu saying no diplomatic agreement was possible with Iran's leadership, while Trump sought a negotiated end to the months-long conflict. 
 
 'It's still unclear whether Netanyahu will pay for what happened during his time in office'

Voter warning  
The endorsement comes after US Secretary of State Marco Rubio warned against a brewing "crisis" in the occupied West Bank after an American photojournalist for The Washington Post was injured in a brutal attack by Israeli settlers. 
"We're very disturbed by those images and what we're seeing," Rubio told reporters Saturday. Netanyahu's office said it was investigating the circumstances around the attack. 
With Israel and Netanyahu looking increasingly isolated on the world stage, Trump's support is vital. 
Netanyahu, who turns 77 on October 21, is Israel's longest-serving prime minister, having served on and off for more than 19 years. 
The wily political operator returned to power in December 2022, bringing in once-shunned ultra-nationalists and quickly tried to rein in the judiciary, which is examining corruption charges that could land him in jail. 
His main election rival is opposition politician Gadi Eisenkot, the leader of the centre-right Yashar party and a former military chief who regularly accuses Netanyahu of bearing personal responsibility for the October 7 attack. 
About seven million Israelis will be eligible to vote in the legislative election. 
Read moreIsrael denounces Macron's UN remarks 
Current polls show that neither Netanyahu's bloc nor that led by Eisenkot is in a position to win the 61 seats needed to control the 120-seat parliament and form a governing coalition. 
Eisenkot said that only Israelis could choose who they want to run the country. 
Speaking at a conference in Tel Aviv, Eisenkot said he "admires" Trump "but Israel is a democratic country, only Israelis can choose their leaders". 
But Trump warned against Israel electing "anyone other than Bibi", writing that if voters chose one of his rivals, "America will have to do this work ourselves, and I am not inclined to do so". 
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

Published: 1:04am, 19 Oct 2026Updated: 11:17am, 19 Oct 2026

US President Donald Trump on Sunday endorsed his ally Benjamin Netanyahu as the long-time Israeli prime minister struggles for an edge in next week’s parliamentary election.

Trump praised Netanyahu as a “great warrior prime minister” and peace partner, crediting him with joining the United States in launching strikes on Iran in February. The conflict, in its seventh month, has disrupted energy markets globally and wreaked havoc across the Middle East, damaging critical infrastructure and destabilising regional ‌economies.

“Bibi Netanyahu has been Strong, Brave, and Brilliant in the face of tremendous opposition, including that coming from even Israel, itself,” Trump wrote in a post on Truth Social.

“Despite all of that, he has endured and, in fact, he has thrived! I have watched Bibi under the most trying of times. Normal men or women in such situations would have wilted under the pressure – But Bibi did not wilt, he actually got stronger, and maintains that same Strength today.”

In his message, addressed to “the Great People of Israel”, Trump added: “Please let this Letter serve to represent my Complete and Total Endorsement of Bibi Netanyahu in his upcoming Race for Re-Election as Prime Minister of Israel”.

The Trump endorsement is ⁠not certain to give Netanyahu and his right-wing Likud party a boost in the October 27 national election, as Israeli public support for Trump has diminished amid Israeli-US disagreements over Iran.

People cross a bridge beneath a campaign advertisement featuring Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, right, and his main rival, opposition candidate Gadi Eisenkot. Photo: AP

Polls have ‌suggested no candidate has a clear path to power. Israel’s prime minister is chosen through coalition-building in parliament rather than by direct popular vote.

It will be Israel’s first vote since the Hamas attack on October 7, 2023, that shook the country and plunged the Middle East into turmoil, as ‌Israel went to war in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran.

The election could determine whether Netanyahu remains in power after one of the most consequential periods in Israel’s history, ⁠or is defeated by centrist rivals promising ⁠to usher in a new era.

Netanyahu promptly expressed his thanks to his “dear friend Donald” on X, saying: “Together we will complete the mission!”

Trump has broken with long-time US tradition by endorsing candidates in elections in foreign countries including Hungary, Colombia, Argentina, ‌Japan and Honduras.

Trump’s relationship with Netanyahu has been close but also fractious, with the president at times publicly and privately criticising Israel’s longest-serving prime minister.

US President Donald Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu at the Israeli parliament, the Knesset, in Jerusalem on October 13, 2025. Photo: AFP

The war that the US and Israel launched against Iran is unpopular with Americans, ‌who ‌vote November 3 in congressional elections, while support for Israel among Americans has also decreased over the Iran war and Israel’s conduct in the three-year war in Gaza that Trump has promised ‌to end. Both leaders on Sunday mentioned finishing the job in Iran.

Tamar Hermann, a senior research fellow at the non-partisan Israel Democracy Institute in Jerusalem, said Trump’s late endorsement could help win ⁠back wavering Netanyahu voters but was unlikely to draw widespread support.

Most Israelis, even those who are critical of Netanyahu and his government, were largely in favour of the Iran war.

In an ⁠election this close, “it couldn’t hurt him, and it might help,” said analyst Aaron David Miller of the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace in Washington.

Netanyahu’s religious-nationalist coalition is projected to lose its governing majority, although the opposition may also struggle to form a government, opinion polls show. That could lead to Netanyahu serving as a caretaker prime minister ‌while another election is held.

The US president passed ‌up earlier opportunities to endorse Netanyahu, perhaps because he wanted to see what leverage he could exercise on issues like Gaza or Lebanon, said Miller. In the end, he said, Trump sided with a leader he sees as strong and unfairly persecuted.

“However angry Trump may be at Netanyahu for pushing this Iran war, this in the end was a Trump decision,” Miller added.

A Trump decision not to endorse Netanyahu would have raised “legitimate questions about whether or not the whole Iran venture was in fact something Trump should have done,” he said.

sources.text: US President Donald Trump has written a glowing endorsement of the Israeli prime minister just months after labelling him "crazy" and days after suggesting he does not trust him.In a lengthy post on his Truth Social platform, Mr Trump urged Israelis to vote for Benjamin Netanyahu and his Likud party in their upcoming election, now just over a week away.He labelled the Israeli prime minister a "Great Warrior Prime Minister, and an even greater Partner for Peace", pointing to the decision the pair took to launch their war against Iran on February 28.Negotiations to end that conflict have been stalled for months, despite Mr Trump's repeated insistence Iran has been defeated."If Israel has the wrong Leader, which would be anyone other than Bibi, America will have to do this work ourselves, and I am not inclined to do so," he wrote."Bibi Netanyahu has been Strong, Brave, and Brilliant in the face of tremendous opposition, including that coming from even Israel, itself.Donald Trump and Benjamin Netanyahu have dinner at the White House in 2025. (Reuters: Kevin Lamarque)"Despite all of that, he has endured and, in fact, he has thrived!"He said Mr Netanyahu was the partner the US was "demanding of Israel, a Country for which it has done so much"."Please let this Letter serve to represent my Complete and Total Endorsement of Bibi Netanyahu in his upcoming Race for Re-Election as Prime Minister of Israel," Mr Trump said.Benjamin Netanyahu's social media posts says Israel's enemies want him to lose the election while its friends want him to win. (Supplied: Benjamin Netanyahu)Mr Netanyahu seized upon the endorsement, posting an image on social media showing Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas, Iran's reclusive Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani along with the caption: "Israel's enemies want Netanyahu to lose."It was accompanied by an image of the Israeli prime minister and Mr Trump, and the caption: "A friend of Israel wants Netanyahu to win."Trump changes tuneIn June, the US president unleashed an expletive-laden tirade against Mr Netanyahu as he effectively accused him of trying to undermine the prospects of a deal with Iran.During a fiery phone call, after the Israeli prime minister ordered strikes on central Beirut against Iranian-backed Hezbollah, Mr Trump said Mr Netanyahu was "f***ing crazy" and said he would be in jail had it not been for his efforts to protect him.Mr Netanyahu is subject to an arrest warrant from the International Criminal Court (ICC) for alleged war crimes — something the US has condemned the court for pursuing, issuing sanctions against its officials in response.The Israeli prime minister is also embroiled in a long-running corruption case at home, which is still before the local courts.Mr Trump has previously urged Israeli President Isaac Herzog to pardon the prime minister, which he has to this point refused to do.On Friday, during an interview with US network Newsmax, Mr Trump talked up the success of his relationship with Mr Netanyahu.But when expressly asked whether he trusted the man, he replied: "I don't trust anybody in the world of politics."Netanyahu vying for re-electionMr Netanyahu is facing the challenge of his political life in the upcoming October 27 election, with polling suggesting his Likud party could be the second largest in the Israeli Knesset, behind challenger Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar party.However, he could retain the prime ministership after such a result, given the need for complicated coalition negotiations to establish a working majority and secure power.The relationship between the US and Israel, and their leaders, has been a focus of campaigning during the election, with some of Mr Netanyahu's opponents accusing him of weakening the ties with Israel's closest ally.Reports emerged earlier this month that the Trump administration had encouraged Israel to launch unilateral attacks against Iran, shattering the relative calm that had persisted for months, because the US president did not want to return to all-out war before the US midterm elections in November.Mr Netanyahu is Israel's longest serving prime minister.

Normal men or women in such situations would have wilted under the pressure – But Bibi did not wilt, he actually got stronger, and maintains that same Strength today.”In his message, addressed to “the Great People of Israel”, Trump added: “Please let this Letter serve to represent my Complete and Total Endorsement of Bibi Netanyahu in his upcoming Race for Re-Election as Prime Minister of Israel.”The Trump endorsement is not certain to give Netanyahu and his right-wing Likud party a boost in the Oct 27 national election, as Israeli public support for Trump has diminished amid Israeli-US disagreements over Iran.Polls have suggested no candidate has a clear path to power. Israel’s prime minister is chosen through coalition-building in Parliament rather than by direct popular vote.It will be Israel’s first vote since the Hamas attack on Oct 7, 2023, that shook the country and plunged the Middle East into turmoil, as Israel went to war in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran.The election could determine whether Netanyahu remains in power after one of the most consequential periods in Israel’s history, or is defeated by centrist rivals promising to usher in a new era.Netanyahu promptly expressed his thanks to Trump on X, saying: “Together we will complete the mission!”Trump has broken with long-time US tradition by endorsing candidates in elections in foreign countries, including Hungary, Colombia, Argentina, Japan and Honduras.Endorsement might helpTrump’s relationship with Netanyahu has been close but also fractious, with the President at times publicly and privately criticising Israel’s longest-serving prime minister.The war that the US and Israel launched against Iran is unpopular with Americans, who vote on Nov 3 in congressional elections, while support for Israel among Americans has also decreased over the Iran war and Israel’s conduct in the three-year war in Gaza that Trump has promised to end. Both leaders on Sunday mentioned finishing the job in Iran.Tamar Hermann, a senior research fellow at the non-partisan Israel Democracy Institute in Jerusalem, said Trump’s late endorsement could help win back wavering Netanyahu voters but was unlikely to draw widespread support.Most Israelis, even those who are critical of Netanyahu and his government, were largely in favour of the Iran war.In an election this close, “it couldn’t hurt him, and it might help”, said analyst Aaron David Miller of the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace in Washington.Netanyahu’s religious-nationalist coalition is projected to lose its governing majority, although the opposition may also struggle to form a government, opinion polls show. That could lead to Netanyahu serving as a caretaker prime minister while another election is held.The US President passed up earlier opportunities to endorse Netanyahu, perhaps because he wanted to see what leverage he could exercise on issues like Gaza or Lebanon, said Miller. In the end, he said, Trump sided with a leader he sees as strong and unfairly persecuted.“However angry Trump may be at Netanyahu for pushing this Iran war, this in the end was a Trump decision,” Miller added.A Trump decision not to endorse Netanyahu would have raised “legitimate questions about whether or not the whole Iran venture was in fact something Trump should have done”, he said.
